analysis.one_liner: Raises federal employee pay by 4.3% in 2026, including locality pay.
analysis.headline: The bill to raise federal employee pay by 4.3% in 2026 gathered 36 cosponsors but never received a committee vote or floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill sets the annual pay raise for about 2 million federal civilian employees at 3.3% for 2026, plus an extra 1% in locality pay that varies by region. Federal workers' raises are normally set by the President through the budget process, and this bill is Congress's way of trying to lock in a larger raise. It was referred to the Oversight and Government Reform Committee, which never took it up, and it received no vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal civilian employees under the General Schedule and hourly wage-grade workers, roughly 2 million people, would get a 3.3% across-the-board raise in 2026 plus an additional 1% locality adjustment. Workers in higher-cost regions benefit most from the locality piece.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Federal employees, especially in high-cost regions

how_it_helps.text: Raises basic pay under the statutory pay systems by 3.3% for calendar year 2026, and does the same for prevailing-rate (hourly, wage-grade) federal workers, bypassing the normal wage survey rules for that year.
Adds a separate 1% locality pay increase on top of the 3.3%, a total of 4.3%, with the locality component aimed at regions where private-sector pay outpaces federal pay.

A larger raise helps federal workers keep pace with inflation and narrows the gap with private-sector pay for the same jobs, which also affects the government's ability to hire and retain skilled staff.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through the Treasury, bear the cost of higher salaries. Under the mechanism the bill changes, the raise is not offset by cuts anywhere else; it is simply a larger federal payroll expense, in the billions of dollars annually.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers through higher payroll costs

drawbacks.text: The raise is an unreduced federal payroll cost of roughly $20-25 billion a year by outside estimates, and it is not offset by spending cuts or revenue.

Federal pay raises are normally set each year by the President through the budget process, so a statute like this is largely an annual advocacy exercise; the same raise, or a different one, can be set without this bill.

A blanket 3.3% raise goes to all federal employees regardless of whether their pay already matches or exceeds private-sector pay for comparable work, a point critics of across-the-board federal raises have raised in good faith.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly 2 million federal employees affected, this is a straightforward 4.3% raise that keeps their pay closer to private-sector levels. The cost falls on all taxpayers, and because the raise is not targeted, some of it goes to employees in regions where federal pay already matches private pay. The mechanism is blunt but simple, and the real question is political: Congress has not enacted a pay-raise bill like this in over a decade, preferring to let presidential budgets set the number.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Oversight and Government Reform Committee from January 2025 onward with no hearing, markup, or vote, and its original sponsor, Rep. Connolly, who had left the House, was replaced as first sponsor in September 2025 so cosponsors could still be added.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 16, 2025 by Rep. Connolly with six original cosponsors and referred the same day to the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform.
It attracted 36 cosponsors, 35 Democrats and 1 Republican, but the committee never held a markup or scheduled it for a floor vote.

On September 16, 2025, Rep. Walkinshaw was recognized as the new first sponsor so that cosponsors could continue to be added, which is a routine step taken when an original sponsor has left office; the bill still received no committee action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal employees did not receive the larger raise, so the Treasury saved the cost in 2026 unless the number is set higher through the normal budget process. The bill's failure mainly means the annual federal pay raise was left to the President's budget, where it is easier to keep the number smaller.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal workers; taxpayers saved the raise's cost

for.what_they_did: Long supported annual FAIR Act pay-raise legislation and pressed Congress to enact a larger raise than the President's budget proposes.

against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on January 16, 2025 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the session so far.

against.what_they_did: Did not bring the bill to the floor at any point; with a committee-pending bill and no committee action, it never reached a vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's cosponsors were 35 Democrats and just 1 Republican, and with Republicans holding the committee and the floor calendar, no action followed the referral.

industries.industry: Federal employee unions and the federal workforce
industries.note: The bill would have given roughly 2 million federal civilian workers a 4.3% raise in 2026; its failure leaves raises to the President's budget, which has generally proposed smaller numbers. Federal pay levels also matter to taxpayers and to the government's ability to compete for skilled staff.
A larger across-the-board raise is an uncompensated payroll cost of billions of dollars a year; the bill's death means taxpayers did not bear that cost for 2026 through this route.

analysis.trajectory: The bill is highly unlikely to advance. Every FAIR Act pay-raise bill of this kind in recent Congresses has died in committee, and this one has sat untouched for over eight months with no hearing or markup scheduled. Federal pay for 2026 will most likely be set through the President's budget and appropriations process instead.
